title: Just listening
hookLine: kirtan is the singing of the Guru's hymns, and the first practice is simply to listen

cards: There's probably a song you've heard a hundred times and never actually listened to. It plays in the store, in the car, in the background of your life.
Then one day you hear it with headphones, eyes closed, and catch the harmony underneath, a line you never noticed. It's a different song. Now go to the Golden Temple in Amritsar, before dawn.
From the center of the pool, music is already drifting out across the water. Voices, a harmonium, a drum. It goes on almost all day, every day.
People sit along the walkway with their eyes closed. Not singing. Not reading.

teach.b: Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, the shabads of the Guru Granth Sahib, set to music. It's at the heart of Sikh worship.
Think back to day thirty-one: Guru Nanak didn't write his hymns to be read silently. He sang them, with Mardana playing the rebab beside him.
The Gurus were musicians. Most of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by musical mood, which is tomorrow's word. So for Sikhs, the Word comes most fully alive when it's sung.

teach.h: IN THIS AGE, KIRTAN IS HIGHEST.
teach.b: Guru Arjan says it plainly, in paraphrase: in this dark age, kirtan, singing the praises of God, is the highest practice. There's a practical reason too. Music gets past the part of you that argues.
You can resist an idea; it's harder to resist a melody.

But camp three starts not with singing, with listening. The Japji, you'll remember, gives four whole stanzas to listening, and kirtan begins the same way. Before you learn a tune or a word, you let the sound in.
You don't have to understand Gurmukhi, know the raga, or feel anything special.
Just listen, the way you'd listen to a friend telling you something important. Sikhs say the sound itself does something: listening to gurbani with attention is already a kind of remembering.
Over the coming days, you'll move from listening to singing. Today, it's only your ears.

how: In the gurdwara, musicians called ragis sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib while the congregation listens, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar kirtan continues for most of the day and is broadcast live.

o: singing the Guru's hymns, set to music
a silent reading of scripture in the gurdwara
dancing in a circle at a religious festival

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak wrote his hymns to be read silently
he sang them, with Mardana on the rebab.
most of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by musical mood
after the opening prayers, its hymns are grouped by raga.
you must understand Gurmukhi before kirtan can mean anything

games.q: you're new to kirtan and sitting in the gurdwara as the hymn begins. you don't know the words or the tune. what's the first practice?
o: sing along as best you can.
read a translation until you understand it.
close your eyes and just listen.
games.why: kirtan begins with listening. before the tune or the words, you let the sound in.

practice: If you can, play one shabad, any one; many gurdwaras stream their kirtan live, including the Golden Temple, and if you can't, simply listen to the room around you.

Close your eyes, don't try to understand or hum along, and let the sound arrive: the voice, the drum, the pause between phrases. When your mind drifts, come back to the sound, as many times as it takes.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, and for camp three, the practice that begins with simply listening.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: singing the praises of God, the hymns of the Gurus.

carryVoice: Your line: just listen. No phone, no dishes, just ears. Day one hundred four.
